chief_complaint: sudden dense left hemiplegia, slurred speech, and severe hypertension during emotional argument
hpi_details: 61M poorly controlled hypertensive presenting with sudden left hemiplegia, gaze preference toward right, and 4 cm acute putaminal hematoma on head CT.
ideas: He thinks the severe anger and shouting during the argument caused an extreme tension headache and pinched a nerve in his neck.
concerns: He is worried that he will remain paralyzed on his left side and lose his independence, needing someone to care for him permanently.
expectations: He hopes to receive an urgent head scan and emergency medication to bring his blood pressure down and restore movement to his arm and leg.

available_results.value: 4.0 cm acute right putaminal intraparenchymal hematoma with surrounding edema and mild local mass effect

clinical_knowledge.topic: Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (Basal Ganglia) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (Basal Ganglia) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management includes neurocritical monitoring, careful blood-pressure control, evaluation for anticoagulant reversal, and neurosurgical assessment, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden dense left hemiplegia, slurred speech, and severe hypertension during emotional argument
Key HPI features: 61M poorly controlled hypertensive presenting with sudden left hemiplegia, gaze preference toward right, and 4 cm acute putaminal hematoma on head CT.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage Basal Ganglia.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage (Basal Ganglia).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ischemic stroke without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Declining consciousness — signals the hematoma is expanding or causing increased pressure.
management_principles: Admit to a stroke unit or neurocritical-care setting; protect the airway as needed and perform frequent neurologic checks.
For a presenting systolic blood pressure of 150–220 mm Hg, lower it smoothly toward approximately 140 mm Hg while avoiding hypotension; individualize targets for more severe hypertension.
Check coagulation studies and medication history; rapidly reverse any relevant anticoagulant-associated coagulopathy.
Obtain repeat CT for neurologic deterioration or per local protocol, and seek neurosurgical input for hydrocephalus, mass effect, or selected decompression indications.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Poorly controlled high blood pressure causes a small brain artery to rupture, bleeding directly into the brain tissue and causing sudden dense weakness on one side — distinct from ischemic stroke, which is caused by a blockage rather than a bleed.
differentials: Hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke
red_flags: Declining consciousness — signals the hematoma is expanding or causing increased pressure

must_ask.say: What were you doing right before this started — was there any stress or straining?
Which side is weak, and how severe is it?
How controlled has your blood pressure been?
Do you have a headache with this?

history.answer: Doctor, about an hour ago my entire left side suddenly went completely limp and paralyzed, and my speech became terribly slurred.
I was in the middle of a very heated, stressful argument with my business partner when my left arm dropped and I couldn't move my left leg.
I was completely fine and normal until about an hour ago, right around one-thirty in the afternoon.
It is complete weakness where I cannot lift my left arm or leg at all, and the whole left side feels heavy and numb.
The paralysis is strictly on my left side, affecting my left face, left arm, and left leg equally.
It struck suddenly and reached full paralysis within just two or three minutes, and it hasn't improved even a little bit.
I can't lift my arm, hold anything, or stand up at all; my left leg just collapses under me.
It happened out of nowhere during that intense argument, and resting hasn't changed anything.
Yes, my words feel thick and slurred when I try to talk, although I can still understand everything people say to me.
My wife told me the left corner of my mouth is drooping, and my eyes feel like they naturally want to look toward the right.
I have a dull, throbbing headache on the right side of my head that started right when my weakness began, and I feel nauseated.
I don't feel the room spinning, but trying to swallow water feels awkward and difficult right now.
I never lost consciousness or blacked out, though I do feel a bit drowsy and drained.
No, I do not have any neck stiffness, back pain, or electric sensations shooting down my spine.
No, I haven't lost control of my urine or stool, and I don't have any numbness around my groin area.
No shortness of breath, no droopy eyelids, and no double vision.
No, I have never had any muscle twitching, tremors, or shrinking of my muscles.
No, I haven't had any colds, coughing, stomach flu, or diarrhea recently.
No, I don't do repetitive wrist work, rest on my elbows, or sit crouched for long periods.
I have had high blood pressure for five years, but I often forget my medication and my readings usually run quite high.
Aside from hypertension and mildly high cholesterol, I don't have diabetes, heart disease, or an irregular heartbeat.
I eat a normal, well-rounded diet with plenty of meat and produce, and I have never had stomach or bowel surgery.
I thought getting so angry and shouting during that argument just pinched a major nerve in my neck and caused my side to go numb.
I'm terrified that this paralysis won't go away and I'll be stuck in a wheelchair unable to look after myself.
I'm hoping you can scan my head and give me medicine to get my blood pressure under control so my arm and leg can move again.
Just high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol.
I had my appendix removed when I was twenty-two, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I am prescribed lisinopril ten milligrams once a day, but I skip doses frequently when I get busy.
No, I do not take aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, blood thinners, or pain medications.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or imaging dyes.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I only drink one or two glasses of wine socially a month, and I don't use recreational drugs.
I run an independent logistics consultancy and live in a two-story home with my wife.
My father suffered an ischemic stroke in his late sixties, and my mother had long-standing high blood pressure.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 192/104 mmHg, pulse 84 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Patient appears acutely ill and anxious, lying supine on the bed with dense weakness of the left extremities and slurred speech.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and date, though speech is moderately dysarthric; language comprehension is intact.
Conjugate gaze preference toward the right; pupils are 3 mm bilaterally and reactive to light.
Left central facial paresis with left nasolabial fold flattening and mouth droop; tongue protrudes with mild leftward deviation, and gag reflex is intact.
Flaccid left hemiplegia with muscle strength 0/5 in both left arm and left leg; right upper and lower extremities demonstrate full 5/5 strength without atrophy or fasciculations.
Significantly diminished sensation to light touch and pinprick across the left face, left arm, and left leg compared to the right side.
Hypoactive deep tendon reflexes (1+) in the left biceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons with 2+ on the right; positive left Babinski response with dorsiflexion of the great toe.
Coordination testing on the left side cannot be performed due to complete paralysis; right-sided rapid alternating movements and finger-to-nose are normal; gait testing is unsafe and deferred.
Neck is supple without resistance to passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
Normal S1 and S2 heart sounds with a regular rhythm; no cardiac murmurs, carotid bruits, or gallops auscultated.
